entries.title: Digital humans: Character Creator in Studio and a MetaHuman adapter
entries.summary: A character appearance editor right in Studio — face blending, sculpting, skin, makeup, hair, body and outfit try-on — and an adapter that recognises MetaHuman exports with no Unreal at runtime.
body: Character Creator has its own Character workspace. The face blends on an archetype circle, and single parts — nose, mouth, eyes, jaw — get their own handle and are picked with a click in the viewport. Sculpting works by dragging with a brush circle, skin, eye, hair and body sliders update the model live, and one shared history undoes with ⌘Z.

Makeup (lipstick, blush, eyeshadow, stubble) is layered on the skin texture and finds the lips, cheeks and eyelids from the face geometry. Clothing and hairstyles are tried on in the viewport without a build; the build adds LODs for skinned parts, shows a triangle budget and places the character in the game as a unit type in one click.

The MetaHuman adapter reads an ordinary glTF / GLB / FBX export: it recognises the UE5 skeleton and face meshes, assigns material roles, selects the face meshes and counts how many of the 52 ARKit facial channels the model has. *_half corrective joints and forearm twists, as well as the jaw and eyes, follow those channels when the morphs do not already move them. Draco-compressed GLB is decoded by an offline script.
entries.verified: Studio Mac build, CTest 9/9 PASS including vivid_metahuman_adapter on three real MetaHuman exports (Ada, Bruce, Draco-decoded Bruce) and vivid_human_lod; web tests 149/149. Screenshots are native Studio output without retouching.
entries.limits: Not full RigLogic: bulge, in/out, fwd/bck correctives stay in bind pose; groom is cards only; .dna is read only by the offline tool; the Ada export has no tongueOut channel. Makeup placement uses the nearest skin vertices; unusual UVs may need a manual tweak.

entries.author: vivid

entries.title: STRATA: 60 fps on a budget phone and half the memory
entries.summary: The same 20 million-triangle spheres now run at 60 fps on GLES on a Galaxy A05s, the process takes about 440 MB instead of 730, and Vulkan frames got cheaper by rotating the image inside the engine.
body: Same scene: 20 spheres of 1,002,252 triangles each, geometry only, rendering at 1200×540. The hierarchy is cooked on disk ahead of time and loads in about 1.2 s.

The hierarchy reaches coarse levels: when simplifying a group gains almost nothing the builder retries with a larger error, and a sphere's roots are merged down to about 256 triangles. Up to 16 levels. With a 60 k triangle budget STRATA draws about 71 k triangles for 20 spheres; far spheres take a few hundred.

Each sphere's cluster selection is cached while the camera and threshold stay put; selected indices live in an immutable buffer per selection and old ones are freed after 16 frames, so re-uploads never wait on the GPU.

Memory. The full index stream is no longer uploaded to video memory when only compacted selections are drawn; CPU indices are kept compressed, meshlet tables are freed after staging, and content pack pages are returned to the system after copying. Process PSS: 730 → 410–455 MB, native heap: 300 → 85 MB on GLES and 123 MB on Vulkan.

Vulkan. This phone's swapchain is portrait and the compositor rotated every frame itself. The engine now rotates the image with a compute shader before presenting (AIVERSE_VK_PRE_ROTATE=0 turns it off): 43 → 48 fps.
The STRATA corner panel shows triangles, error threshold, draw calls, process memory, CPU indices and selection video memory.
entries.verified: Samsung Galaxy A05s (Adreno 610, 1200×540), 60 k budget: GLES 59.9 fps static and 58.4 fps in a camera fly-through, ~71 k triangles, 20 draw calls, PSS 437 MB. 120 k budget: 54 fps. Vulkan: 48 fps with in-engine rotation, 43 without. Without STRATA: 4.5 fps.
entries.limits: Vulkan is still slower than GLES and does not draw the panel text. About 200 MB of video memory is 60-byte vertices and the original index buffer of models drawn only through STRATA; compressing them is next. About 100 MB is the .apk mapping; the effect of releasing pages on file reads is not measured yet.

media.caption: Galaxy A05s, GLES: 20 spheres of a million triangles each, 60 fps
The same frame on Vulkan with in-engine pre-rotation, 48 fps

entries.author: strata

entries.title: STRATA: cooked geometry on disk, a working hierarchy and a first phone measurement
entries.summary: STRATA cluster hierarchies are now built ahead of time and stored next to the content: the game loads them in a fraction of a second instead of minutes. Bugs that kept STRATA from simplifying geometry were found and fixed, and an automatic triangle budget was added.
body: The test scene is 20 bumpy spheres of 1,002,252 triangles each (4 different models), about 20 M triangles in total, with no terrain, sky or interface: geometry only. The camera stands next to the nearest sphere and the row recedes into the distance.

Cooking. The aiverse_strata_cook tool builds the cluster hierarchy of every model in a scene and writes it to the geometry scene's strata.cooked folder. A file is tied to its source geometry and the builder version: if the model changes the file is ignored and the hierarchy is built as before. Loading 4 spheres takes 0.4 s on a Mac and about 1.2 s on a phone instead of roughly 6 minutes of building per sphere.

The hierarchy. Leaf clusters were cut in file order and came out as strips with almost every vertex on a border; borders stay locked while simplifying, so the tree stalled: a sphere's coarsest level still had 743 k triangles. Clusters are now compact patches and a group's error tolerance follows its children's size. A sphere's coarsest level is 13 k triangles, and STRATA draws 1.1 M triangles in 20 draw calls instead of 19.4 M.
Cluster selection is cheaper: errors are computed only for nodes the traversal reaches, clusters outside the view are not refined, and the index set is uploaded again only when the selection changes.

The triangle budget (strata.triangleBudget or AIVERSE_STRATA_TRI_BUDGET) raises the error threshold while there are more triangles than the budget. A corner panel shows the STRATA route, whether data came from disk, triangles, threshold, draw calls, memory and frame time; a window on the right shows the clusters coloured by detail level.
Every object of the scene can choose its drawing path in the editor: Auto (STRATA or ordinary LODs per model), STRATA or LOD — in the Static geometry window or the object's strata field.
entries.verified: Mac Studio (M3 Ultra, Metal): 1.1 M triangles and 20 draw calls versus 20 M without STRATA. Samsung Galaxy A05s (Adreno 610, rendering at 1200×540): no budget 16 fps on Vulkan and 20 fps on GLES; with a 250 k triangle budget 35 and 45 fps; without STRATA 4 fps.
entries.limits: No 60 fps on this phone yet: frame time grows almost linearly with triangles, and in the measurement the builder stopped at 8 levels so STRATA could not go below about 270 k triangles for 20 spheres; the limit is now 16 levels, not yet re-measured. Vulkan is slower than GLES on this phone; the cause is not found yet. The process takes about 750 MB: indices are kept whole and vertices are 60 bytes. Disk streaming of index pages exists but was not enabled in this scene.

media.caption: 20 spheres of a million triangles each; on the right the clusters, coloured by detail level
The same frame: every cluster in its own colour
Galaxy A05s, Vulkan: 250 k triangle budget, 35 fps

entries.title: Depth of field and motion blur are regular effects
entries.summary: Depth of field and motion blur are no longer experimental: add the effect to a camera profile and it works on Metal, OpenGL and Vulkan.
body: Both effects used to need an environment variable. Now `depthOfField` and `motionBlur` in a project's `postfx` or a camera profile work right away, like bloom or colour grading. They default to the High quality tier, motion blur needs an HDR frame. `AIVERSE_PRISMA_DOF=0` and `AIVERSE_PRISMA_MOTION_BLUR=0` remain to turn them off.

Depth of field works from hardware depth or from distance in metres along the camera (`metricFocus`); LENS sets the focus from lens parameters. Motion blur follows camera motion and the velocity of moving objects.
entries.verified: The same HDR scene on Metal and OpenGL (Mac) and on Vulkan (Android, Adreno 610): focused on the scene the frame stays sharp, focused near the camera it blurs clearly; a turning camera with motion blur smears the frame, a still one is left alone. PRISMA's report marks each effect as drawn.
entries.limits: An approximation, not a physical lens model: no hexagonal bokeh or depth layer separation. On weak mobile GPUs both stay off by default below the High tier.

Focus near the camera: the whole scene is soft, Metal
Camera turning without motion blur, Metal
The same turn with motion blur, Metal

entries.author: prisma

entries.title: AO, reflections, lens effects, SMAA and FSR
entries.summary: PRISMA gains ambient occlusion, screen-space reflections, lens flare and dirt, distortion, anamorphic streaks, halation, heat haze with shockwaves, SMAA, FSR 1 upscaling and histogram exposure.
body: The new effects go into a project's, map's or camera profile's `postfx`, like bloom: `ambientOcclusion`, `screenSpaceReflections`, `lensFlare` (with a dirt texture or procedural smudges), `lensDistortion` (barrel, pincushion, Panini), `anamorphicStreaks`, `halation`, `heatHaze`, `smaa`, `fsr`. Auto exposure can meter from a luminance histogram (`histogram`, low and high percentiles), so a bright sky or a dark corner no longer throws exposure off.

AO and reflections work from the depth buffer: normals are reconstructed from depth, reflections are found by marching a ray through the scene. FSR 1 (EASU + RCAS) renders the 3D scene at a lower resolution and scales it to the screen; a DLSS route exists, but its NGX adapter has not been built yet. A `sceneColor` node in Shader Graph lets post effects read the frame; the stylization presets use it: toon, sketch, CRT, scanlines, dithering, Kuwahara.
Every effect has quality tiers and a cost estimate, and PRISMA's report shows whether it was drawn.
entries.verified: Mac Studio (M3 Ultra), commit b7bf96e9: 18 tests on Metal (each of the 12 effects is drawn and changes the frame the expected way, plus the PRISMA data and Shader Graph tests) and 12 on OpenGL — all passed. On Linux the same 12 scenes passed on Vulkan (software lavapipe). The first Mac run found banding in AO, broken-up reflections, an upside-down FSR frame on Metal and smeared streaks — fixed before this run.
entries.limits: DLSS was not built or tested (needs Windows, RTX and the NGX SDK). Vulkan was checked only on a software renderer, not on real GPUs or Android. AO and SSR work from depth without a G-buffer: surfaces reflect by normal slope, not by material; thin objects may be noisy. GPU cost was not measured.

media.caption: AO: without (left) and with ambient occlusion — contact shadows under the spheres and cubes, Metal
Screen-space reflections on the floor: without and with SSR, Metal
Lens flare ghosts from a bright lamp and an anamorphic streak, Metal
Film halation and lens distortion with Panini, Metal

entries.author: prisma

entries.title: Planets on TerraWeave: relief, biomes, trees and rocks
entries.summary: Planet relief is now built by TerraWeave fields carried over to the sphere, and TerraWeave trees and rocks grow on land according to the climate of each place.
body: The planet generator (rocky, ocean and moon presets) takes heights and biomes from TerraWeave: the same octave sum and climate model as on flat maps, with the fields evaluated in 3D on the sphere. Cube faces therefore join without seams, and the poles are colder than the equator.

Trees and rocks now cover the land: spruce and pine in cold places, oak and birch in forests and grassland, willow in wetlands, boulders and slabs in deserts and on rock. The models come from the Arbor tree generator and the TerraWeave rock generator; the place and species for every cell are chosen deterministically. Density and scale are set in the map with visual.flora.
entries.verified: Frames taken in the game client (OpenGL) on the regenerated Big Planet; generator checks — face seams, separated starts, symmetry and determinism — pass with the new reference hashes.
entries.limits: Planet seas are still their own, not NEREID: no waves or shore foam yet. Trees ignore fog of war, and the Metal shaders have not been run on a Mac yet.

media.caption: The coast up close: TerraWeave trees on land, the shore left clear
Big Planet from orbit: relief and seas from TerraWeave fields

entries.author: planets

entries.title: Planet seas became NEREID water bodies
entries.summary: The sea of any sphere — a planet, a moon or anything else — is now a NEREID water body: depth, up, current, waves and buoyancy follow the radius, and ships get splashes and wakes.
body: NEREID gained sphere water bodies: a shell around the planet's centre with the surface at sea level and the floor at a set depth. For any point they return the radial depth, the direction up from the centre and a current flowing east around an axis.

The same buoyancy components as for flat water push an object along the radius on a sphere. A map turns this on with a single nereid key on a body; without the key nothing is registered, and saves and checksums of old maps stay the same. Big Planet already has it on.

Waves now exist in the simulation too: the sea level on a sphere rises and falls with a set amplitude and period, and depth and buoyancy follow it. Objects in the water get entry, exit and wake events — the same as for flat water, so splash effects read them unchanged. This is shared NEREID code for any game, not only strategy: one flag in the water pipeline turns it on.
entries.verified: The new ecs_nereid_sphere_water_test (sampling, current, buoyancy, determinism, saves) passes; a bot match on Big Planet plays to a winner, the save restore check passes, and the planets template checksums match the baseline.
entries.limits: Simulation waves and the waves on screen do not match exactly yet: the picture has its own, the simulation its own. Built-in RTS ships get probes automatically but do not drift with the current yet — movement stays with the host.
entries.author: planets

entries.title: Planet seas on NEREID waves
entries.summary: Water on planets is now drawn with NEREID's wave model — the same as rivers and lakes on flat maps: turquoise shallows, deep blue and foam along the coast.
body: NEREID's waves moved into a shared set of shader functions used by both flat water and planet seas. On a sphere the same waves are evaluated in three projections and blended by the surface direction, so cube faces show no seams.
The sea colour follows the depth under every point: light and clear near the shore, darker further out. Foam runs along the land's edge, and the edge itself follows the relief.
entries.verified: Frames taken in the game client (OpenGL) on Big Planet; flat water on an ordinary map draws as before after the functions moved.
entries.limits: This is the look. NEREID water bodies on spheres do not exist yet: planet seas have no buoyancy, currents or water contact so far. The shader has not been run on Metal yet.

media.caption: A planet coast: shallow water, foam along the edge and TerraWeave trees
Lakes from orbit: colour by depth and a light rim

entries.author: planets

entries.title: Planets: coasts that follow the relief instead of square seas
entries.summary: The sea on a planet is now cut by the ground height at every pixel, and the Big Planet map is built by the engine's generator: noise relief, bays and islands.
body: Big Planet used to have seas with straight edges. The cause was the map itself: its heights came from a hand-made formula with latitude bands, and lowlands on the cube faces came out rectangular. The map is now built by the engine's generator with the rocky preset — the same one as in the Generation window: noise relief, sea level by water share, flat base areas and fair starts.

The water itself is neater too: every sea pixel checks whether the ground under it is above sea level, and the water turns shallow towards the coast. The coastline follows the relief exactly at any level of detail and no longer depends on depth buffer precision.
entries.verified: Frames taken in the game client (OpenGL); a bot match on the new map plays to a winner.
entries.limits: The Metal shader is updated but has not been run on a Mac yet. The small Two Worlds map keeps its old heights for now: tests depend on it.

media.caption: Big Planet from the generator: bays, islands and shallow water at the coast
The same planet from orbit
Before: a square sea on the old map

entries.author: planets

entries.title: PHYSIS: tornadoes
entries.summary: PHYSIS now has tornadoes: defined in map data, they follow a path or wander, twist the wind, fan and snuff fire, tear up debris and deal damage.
body: A tornado is an entry of the tornadoes array in the map's physis block: centre, core and outer radius, height, spin, updraft and inflow, start and lifetime, spin-up and decay. The path is a straight drift, a wander inside bounds, or waypoints, looping or once.

The vortex changes PHYSIS wind, so everything that reads the wind feels it: forces, load on vegetation and buildings, grass, particles. It snuffs fire at the centre and fans it in the ring around. Debris is torn up at the base, carried by the wind and falls. Light game objects with NatureCarriable are lifted and carried away. Units and buildings take damage through a common environment hook, already connected in RTS.

On screen a tornado is a dust funnel with a dust ring at the ground and flying debris, with a positional roar, strong wind in the grass and choppy water nearby. The example is the Tornado Valley map of the skirmish template.
entries.verified: Game client on a Mac (Metal), Tornado Valley map: the tornado follows its path with 9 to 24 pieces of debris in the frame. A match with one seed repeats with the same checksum; replay and restore from a save match.
entries.limits: Only RTS games take tornado damage so far. Debris does not collide with anything. Grass bending, water and sound were not checked separately. The funnel is simple — a project can replace the effect with its own fx/physis_tornado.json.

media.caption: A tornado on the Tornado Valley map
Wide view: the tornado crossing the valley

entries.author: physis

entries.title: A battle on one animation graph
entries.summary: Ninety characters, each with its own instance of one MotionWeave graph: ranks march and run, the front line fights, some have already fallen.
body: One graph for everyone: a state machine (march → fight → dead), a walk/run blend, breathing on top of the motion and the attack applied to the upper body only, so the legs stand or walk meanwhile. Each character gets its own parameters and clock offset, so the ranks never move in step.
The sword is not baked into the model: every frame it takes the hand position from the evaluated pose. The team colour goes onto the cloth through the material, with no separate model per army.
entries.verified: Captured on Linux through OpenGL: a 1920×1080 frame and a 1280×720 two-second clip. 90 characters: 63 marching, 21 fighting, 6 fallen.
entries.limits: Not captured on Metal. The model is the simple one from the engine template; retargeting to other rigs and skeleton LODs are not shown in this frame.

media.caption: Two ranks meet: every character runs its own graph instance
Two seconds of the battle: every character moves by its own graph instance

entries.title: LUMA on Vulkan and Android: direct light, dynamic GI and camera-following cascades
entries.summary: Luma and dynamic GI now run on Vulkan and are checked on an Android phone, and GI cascades follow the camera through large worlds.
body: Luma — direct lighting for thousands of point and spot lights with geometry shadows, GGX reflections and temporal denoising — used to run on Metal only. The same computation now runs on Vulkan, so Luma runs on Android, and on Windows and Linux when Vulkan is selected.

Dynamic GI has a `"scroll": true` mode: up to three probe cascades follow the camera in whole cells. Probes that stay keep their light, cells entering the volume are cleared and traced again — stale light from another place is never shown. The geometry around the camera is loaded as it moves. GI stays on screen while probes update.
TerraWeave terrain tiles feed dynamic GI as soon as they are built.
entries.verified: Samsung Galaxy A05s phone (Adreno 610, Vulkan): Luma in 9 scenes (diffuse, metal, PBR, spot lights, shadows) and dynamic GI on CPU and GPU, with three cascades and with the camera moving away and back, match the CPU reference. The same scenes are checked on Metal.
entries.limits: On Android these are test scenes, not a game: performance on weak phones has not been measured. CPU GI cascades do not scroll.

media.caption: 128 Luma point lights on a floor, Vulkan on Android
The same light on a metal floor: GGX reflection, Vulkan on Android

entries.author: lighting

entries.title: Luma: area lights, particle lights and object motion
entries.summary: Luma handles sphere and tube lights, takes particle lights and uses object motion in its temporal smoothing; on the way, object motion vectors started working on Metal.
body: Besides point and spot lights Luma now lights with spheres and tubes (bulbs, neon tubes). A sphere lights like its centre, without blowing up when the surface is inside it; a tube lights from the point of its axis nearest the surface. Highlights widen with the source's apparent size. In the editor and over MCP a light takes type `sphere` or `tube` with a radius and a length.

Particle lights can be handed to Luma every frame with stable per-particle keys (`fx::appendLumaFxLights`, `LumaHost::setDynamicLights`). When Luma does not draw direct light, particles keep going to the regular light system — light is never added twice.

Luma's temporal smoothing takes the velocity of moving objects from PRISMA, so light on them does not smear. The check showed that on Metal object velocity was not computed at all: two motion-vector shaders did not compile. That is fixed: on Metal PRISMA effects now get the velocity of moving models.
entries.verified: Mac Studio (Metal): `ctest -L Lighting` — Luma in all 12 scenes, including a moving slab with motion blur, a sphere and a tube. Samsung Galaxy A05s phone (Adreno 610, Vulkan): the same 12 scenes match the reference. The CPU reference (`lumaweave_direct_reference`) checks the sphere, the tube, GPU packing and particle keys.
entries.limits: Area lights are approximate: a tube lights from one nearest point rather than integrating along its length, and there are no rectangular lights. No host feeds particles into Luma yet: Studio has no particles and the game client does not use Luma — only the API is ready.

media.caption: A Luma tube light over a floor, Vulkan on Android
A sphere light with the surface inside the sphere, Vulkan on Android

entries.author: lighting

entries.title: Baked lighting on Vulkan and Android
entries.summary: Baked lightmaps and light probes are checked on Vulkan and Android; on the way, reading packed vertex data on mobile GPUs was fixed — it broke both lightmaps and skeletal animation.
body: Static models standing where they were baked take their light from the lightmap, moved or new objects from the probe grid. This has long worked on Metal and GL; the same is now checked on Vulkan and on an Android phone.

The check found a bug in the Vulkan backend. Some mobile GPUs (Adreno 610 among them) have no `R8G8B8A8_USCALED` vertex format, so byte attributes were read as 0..1 instead of 0..255. Lightmap UVs pointed at one spot and skeletal animation used the wrong bones. On such devices the engine now builds a vertex-shader variant that restores the real values; devices with the format are unchanged.
The tests of the new PRISMA effects were fixed too: their check did not recognise the "PASS" line and reported passing effects as failed.
entries.verified: New GPU test `lighting_baked_{gpu,gl,vulkan}`: a slab with a two-colour lightmap and the same slab moved (lit by probes), sun off. Mac Studio (Metal and GL) and a Samsung Galaxy A05s phone (Adreno 610, Vulkan) — passed. On the phone the lightmap UV check failed before the fix and passes after; Luma, dynamic GI and `aiverse_vulkan_tests` pass there again.
entries.limits: This is a one-slab test scene, not baking a real map on a phone. Skeletal models on Adreno were not checked visually — the fix is verified on lightmaps and on compiling the shader variants.

media.caption: A two-colour lightmap on a slab: red on the left, blue on the right, Vulkan on Android
The same slab moved off its baked place — lit by a green probe grid

entries.author: lighting

entries.title: LENS: split-screen, director and visibility layers
entries.summary: Two cameras share the screen and each has its own processing — for example a colour main view next to a black-and-white one. A camera can skip whole layers of the scene. The director blends smoothly from one camera to another when priorities change.
body: Split-screen, overlays and picture-in-picture are assembled in one screen pass. PRISMA post-processing can now be set per camera: grading, grain, vignette, depth of field. Lens exposure and focus are kept.

Scene objects have visibility layers, cameras have a layer mask; in a scene it is the layers key of a model instance. In the frame the left camera sees a sword on layer 2, the right camera with a mask without that layer does not draw it; without the mask the sword appears on the right too.

The director picks the highest-priority camera and, on a switch, blends position, rotation and field of view from the old camera to the new one. The strip shows frames before the switch, in the middle of the blend and after it.
entries.verified: All frames rendered on a Mac (Metal) in Sponza at 1920×1080. The 1 s director blend was checked by its weights: 0.07 / 0.50 / 0.93 / 1.00 at frames 10 / 20 / 30 / 40.
entries.limits: Layers filter models only; meshes, sprites, terrain and particles ignore the mask, and layers are not available in HLOD scenes. Studio does not edit layers or per-camera post-processing yet. Backends other than Metal are not checked in a frame.

media.caption: Split-screen: left, a colour view with a sword on layer 2; right, another camera with its own black-and-white processing and a mask without that layer — no sword
The same pair without the mask: the right camera sees the sword too
Director: before the switch, the middle of the blend, the new camera

entries.author: lens

entries.title: LENS: panoramas, mirrors, portals and stereo
entries.summary: A camera can capture six cube faces and assemble them into a 360° panorama, show the view of a mirror or a portal clipped at its plane, and render a pair of eyes for stereo — including from the eye poses and field-of-view angles an XR runtime provides.
body: The panorama is built on the GPU from six 90° faces into an equirectangular projection, for reflections, previews and environment capture. A bug was found and fixed: the panorama used to come out upside down. The sun shadow in all six faces comes from one shared shadow map around the capture point, so lighting does not jump at the seams between faces.
Mirror and portal cameras reflect or carry over the main camera's view and clip everything behind the mirror plane or the portal exit. In the frames they are shown as an inset over the main view.
A stereo pair can come from one camera — by interpupillary distance and convergence distance — or from headset data: a pose per eye and four field-of-view tangents, asymmetric ones included.
entries.verified: All frames rendered on a Mac (Metal) in Sponza at 1920×1080: a 360° panorama from 512×512 faces, mirror and portal cameras as insets, stereo pairs from one camera and from XR-runtime-style data.
entries.limits: OpenXR is not connected: headset output, swapchain, frame submission and reprojection stay with an XR host, and nothing has run on a headset. Mirrors and portals are shown as separate views, without a ready mirror surface in the scene. Backends other than Metal are not checked in a frame.

media.caption: A 360° panorama from six cube faces captured in the centre of the Sponza courtyard
Inset: a mirror camera on a plane across the gallery shows its reflection
Inset: the view through a portal whose exit stands in the courtyard
A stereo pair from one camera: 65 mm interpupillary distance, convergence at 4 m
Eyes from XR-runtime-style data: a pose per eye and asymmetric field-of-view angles

entries.author: lens

entries.title: Camera presets: one line of data
entries.summary: Cameras of every project are now built from the same bodies — map overview, follow, chase, first person and planet orbit — and any of them can be set with a ready preset in one line.
body: The map camera, the camera following a hero, the camera behind a car and the first-person view used to live in different places, each configured its own way. Now they are four bodies of one LENS camera system, and a camera block starts from a preset: "camera": {"preset": "overhead-isometric"} gives an isometric view, "topDown": {"camera": {"preset": "follow-speed"}} a camera that pulls back and leads at speed. Any key on top of the preset overrides it.

Eleven presets are ready: a perspective map view, a steep view, a pixel-perfect top view for sprite games, isometric, four follow variants (over the shoulder, straight down, with speed, telephoto from far away), two chase variants and first person. Presets are data; a new one needs no code.

The ECS camera rig gained chase and first-person modes on the same math, and a follow rig with a follow block in cameras.json works like the game follow camera — with a preset, velocity lead and bounds. The Studio cameras window applies a preset in one pick, and agents get the list through the MCP tool lens_camera_presets. The planet camera became the system's fifth body — an orbit over a sphere. The preset and key list is on the documentation page “LENS: camera behaviours”.
entries.verified: macOS, Metal: frames captured in the game client on two templates (only the preset line in game.json changes) and on a planet map with the orbit camera. Camera, LENS MCP tool, top-down and FPS tests pass on Mac.
entries.limits: The ECS follow body leads its target by velocity only: a scene has no stick. The chase camera and first-person look read rules and maps, not cameras.json.

entries.title: One engine for every game: no split by genre
entries.summary: Strategy games, shooters, races and cities now run through one core, GameCore: gameplay systems live in engine/, and project data, not a genre module, decides what is on.
body: The engine used to keep two separate hosts: modules/rts for grid games and modules/fps for metre maps. Every system of the grid host (combat, economy, traffic, driving, arsenal, raids, commerce, careers, sensors, progression) moved to engine/game, the view to engine/view/game, sound and effects to engine/audio and engine/fx.

Actor systems (characters, weapons, projectiles, vehicles, battle royale, races, bots) are now part of the same core: GameCore runs them when the map is in world coordinates. A map of either kind is one scene document; the editor and Studio treat it the same way, and there is one client.

Data-format names no longer name a genre: game.json "module" is "game" or "actor", the actor rules block is "actor", the native Lua library is core, and the bot packages are bots-commander, bots-combatant and action-bots.
entries.verified: Full Mac build and 432 of 433 tests (the failing TA importer wrote the old module name; fixed); checksums of every sample match the previous ones except the known boss_arena seed 2.
entries.limits: Old projects, replays and saves with the previous names do not load. Board, Motion, Voxel and Strategic are still separate hosts; the GTA2 port is separate work.

entries.title: Digital humans: soft facial shadows with adaptive resolution
entries.summary: Shadow map resolution follows the character's size on screen, and the studio light gives a soft portrait shadow — no steps on the neck or ragged edge by the nose.
body: A shared CPU AdaptiveShadowResolution policy picks a 1024, 2048 or 4096 shadow map from viewport height, camera distance and field of view and the share of the frame the character covers. It upgrades at 15% excess demand and downgrades only after 60 frames of low demand, so the resolution does not jump.
The VIVID portrait key light uses soft PCF instead of the general PCSS: an artistic facial filter, not a physically exact area light. Gameplay lighting and shaders are unchanged.
entries.verified: CTest adaptive_shadow_resolution: 1/1 PASS in Release with assertions; native VIVID Creator and Studio builds; video of 168 frames at 1500×920, 24 fps, 0 pipeline failures. Frames are native output without retouching.
entries.limits: The density estimate is conservative, not per pixel; these are not cascaded or virtual shadow maps. Lower resolution tiers at full body are not confirmed with this asset.

entries.author: vivid

entries.title: TERRA ground without tiling or blotches
entries.summary: Up close the ground samples grass, sand and rock from shared world-space detail layers instead of the baked tile texture; a second rotated lookup and macro noise break the repeat.
body: Previously a 64 m tile was baked into a 1024 px texture (about 6 cm per pixel) with top-down grass, which stretched into blotches on slopes. Now the tile texture only stores layer weights (bilinear) and the 4 m detail layers use dominant-axis projection, so slopes do not stretch.

Against tiling, grass and sand get a second lookup rotated ~53° and rescaled, mixed by world gradient noise, plus a two-octave brightness variation (23 m and 7 m). The graph stays within 16 samples; material graphs gain a nodeBudget of up to 192 nodes.
entries.verified: Mac (Metal), AlpineValley review copy: close-up bank frames; shader_graph test (nodeBudget).
entries.limits: Enabled on the review copy; the main AlpineValley project still uses baked textures.

entries.title: TerraWeave forest: a whole tree per draw, impostors in the distance
entries.summary: Identical trees now render as one instanced draw per detail level instead of one draw per branch, and distant trees use impostors baked from the near model.
body: With hierarchical wind a tree becomes one model with three tiers (full, reduced, minimal); FloraView picks the tier and Renderer3D instances identical trees per primitive. A forest frame went from ~6000 draws to 110–177.
The impostor atlas is baked by rasterising the near model with 2×2 supersampling and colour bleeding, so a distant tree keeps its silhouette and crown colour.
entries.verified: Mac (Metal), editor: same-scene draw call and GPU time measurements before/after; tests wind_rig, terraweave_model, terraweave_forest_scene.
entries.limits: Static glTF trees from older exports (as in AlpineValley) still have no LOD chains; horizon-wide impostor grouping is still being verified.

entries.title: The Build panel in Studio
entries.summary: Building a game for a platform and estimating the size of its content now happens right in Studio, on the Publish tab.
body: The panel shows the game name, version and orientation, the platform list (macOS, iOS, Android, Web, Windows, Linux) with already built ones marked, and Release or Debug.

For the selected platform it shows which tools are present, which are missing and which Studio can install itself. "Estimate size" builds only the content pack and lists its size and heaviest files. The build log streams live; the finished build and the log open in Finder.
Studio never builds an unsaved project silently: it offers to save first.

entries.limits: A full platform build from the panel has not been run yet. Branding and the asset audit are still in the old editor only.

entries.title: STRATA: Nanite-style cluster visualization
entries.summary: A debug view shows which clusters STRATA split the geometry into and which detail levels it selected in the frame: every cluster in its own colour.
body: StrataDebugView draws the selected cluster frontier over the frame — fill, wireframe or bounds — coloured by cluster, LOD depth, geometric error or material. Presentation only: LOD selection, routing and GPU data are unchanged, and the view is off by default.

The scene is procedural terrain (≈105 k triangles) and 20 rocks (≈82 k each), about 1.7 M source triangles in total. STRATA selected 15,280 clusters in the frame: small finest-level clusters up close, increasingly coarse ones towards the horizon.
entries.verified: Debug view in main (7d0654223). Frames captured with the tools/site/strata_showcase host (branch feature/site-strata-showcase, 4bf7232d4) on Linux, OpenGL through Mesa llvmpipe: 2 STRATA sources, 0 declined, 15,280 clusters, 1,384,090 debug triangles, 0 truncated, 1920×1080.
entries.limits: Not captured on Metal or other GPUs. Scene triangles are Morton-ordered: with the procedural mesh's original order clusters came out as strips — worth checking on real assets. STRATA rejects Sponza (cross-material seams).

entries.title: SpectraFX: campfires, a portal and fireflies in two scenes
entries.summary: Two scenes for the SpectraFX page: night in Sponza with campfires and a portal, and a sunset with clouds and volumetric fog. Five effects in the ordinary JSON format; particles light the scene.
body: The effects use the ordinary SpectraFX format and live in tools/site/fx_scene/fx. Campfire: a flame body, upright flame tongues, embers with trails, smoke and a warm light. Portal: two counter-rotating spark rings, a glowing rim, an inward swirl and a cold light. Plus rising motes at the portal, fireflies (some with small lights) and low mist.

The particle light module adds point lights to Renderer3D: 9 in the frame, lighting the arches, curtains and floor. PRISMA adds HDR, bloom, colour grading and a vignette; the sunset also uses the physical sky with clouds and god rays and volumetric fog (PRISMA local volumes).
entries.verified: Frames captured with the tools/site/fx_showcase.cpp host (branch feature/site-strata-showcase) on Linux, OpenGL through Mesa llvmpipe, 1920×1080. 6 s of simulation in 1/60 steps, then the frame is frozen. About 1,900 live particles, 9 particle lights. Recipe and commands: tools/site/fx_scene/README.md.
entries.limits: CPU particle backend only, no Metal GPU particles; not captured on Metal. Sponza is the Khronos glTF sample, not a game scene. Found while capturing: PRISMA draws the physical sky over particles seen against the sky, so they vanish — the sunset camera looks down. Trails of particles that only orbit render as vertical streaks.

entries.title: PRISMA: a camera at the water surface — waterline, film and drops
entries.summary: At the surface the frame splits along a waving waterline with a meniscus; after emerging, everything that was under water is covered by a refracting film that drains to the water level, leaving rivulets and drops.
body: lensWater tests the lens point of every pixel against NEREID's waving water plane: underwater optics below the line, the dry image above it, a bright refracting meniscus along it. Nothing runs down the part of the lens that is under water.

After emerging the film clings for the first third of sheetTime, then its ragged edge drains down, leaving meandering rivulets with a head drop and round lens drops with glints that dry over dryTime. Every parameter is tunable and the effect can be disabled.
entries.verified: Mac (Metal), AlpineValley review copy: a real-time dive recording (a frame every ~0.35 s, video assembled at real speed); prisma_lens_water test.
entries.limits: The underside of the surface (total internal reflection) is not rendered separately yet; other backends are not visually verified.

entries.title: Depth of field: the blurred foreground is no longer cut out
entries.summary: Blurred foreground objects now spread over the background as in a real lens instead of ending on a hard line, as if cut out with scissors. The background still does not bleed onto a sharp foreground.
body: Before, blur at a depth boundary threw away everything on the other side: a near curtain or ivy kept a crisp outline over a blurred background, with ghosted patches next to it. Now every point of the frame gathers light from neighbours whose blur disc reaches it. Near blurred objects cover the background and the sharp zone, and what is behind them shows through their edge.

The rule respects sharpness: the background cannot bleed onto an object sharper than itself, so a sharp object in focus keeps a clean edge. The change is in PRISMA's metric depth of field, used by the LENS lens and the metricFocus setting.
entries.verified: A before/after pair was rendered on a Mac (Metal) in Sponza with the same frame: a 35 mm f/1.4 lens focused at 4 m.
entries.limits: The new shader has not been compiled on OpenGL, WebGL or Vulkan yet. The pass is more expensive (32 samples per pixel instead of 8); its cost on weak mobile GPUs has not been measured.

entries.title: NEREID: water turbidity above and below the surface
entries.summary: Water gains a turbidity parameter (with a silt colour): one value changes both the look from above and the visibility when diving.
body: resolvedWaterOptics() turns turbidity into shared extinction, a milky silt colour and a scattering share; both the surface shader and PRISMA's underwater view read them. From above the water uses the real optical path — light down to the bed plus the slanted view ray — so turbid water also looks turbid from outside.
At 0 the water looks as before. The parameter lives in the surface style, the NereidWater component and cascades, is validated and is part of cache keys.
entries.verified: Mac (Metal), AlpineValley review copy: identical frames above and under water at 0 / 0.25 / 0.6; ecs_nereid_renderer_contract test.

entries.title: LENS: the lens sets exposure and depth of field
entries.summary: A camera can be described as a real lens — focal length, aperture, shutter, ISO and focus distance — and the frame gets its exposure and depth of field from them. Smooth camera rails for fly-throughs, camera shake and HDR frame recording to EXR were added.
body: Every camera in cameras.json now has a lens block. With driveExposure and driveDepthOfField on, the camera sets the frame brightness and the sharp zone itself: f/1.4 gives a short sharp zone and a strongly blurred background, f/8 keeps almost everything sharp. It is computed per camera, so the main view and the inset can use different lenses.

For fly-throughs the camera follows a rail through several points at an even speed, eases in and out, and the rail can loop. Shake is noise on six axes with a fade, identical on every run. The old linear rails and the previous shake behave as before.
Frames can be recorded as an OpenEXR sequence with the full HDR range, for editing, grading and render comparisons.
entries.verified: Rendered on a Mac (Metal) in Sponza at 1920×1080: a 35 mm f/1.4 lens focused at 4 m, with a second camera of the same scene in the inset. Exposure, depth of field, rails and EXR maths are covered by tests on Linux and Mac.
entries.limits: HDR recording to EXR is Metal-only for now; OpenGL records an 8-bit frame. Exposure is relative to a default lens, not in physical light units. Cubemaps, panoramas, mirrors, portals and stereo are not done yet.

entries.author: lens

entries.title: Races in any project
entries.summary: A map with a "race" block turns its cars into a race: countdown, gates, laps, standings, bots on the track, a HUD and a chase camera.
body: A race is map data: checkpoint gates in driving order (the last one is the finish), a starting grid and a closed line for the bots. Rules set the countdown, the time to finish after the winner, a timeout and crash damage.

Gates count only in order, so shortcuts gain nothing. A car that is stuck, going the wrong way, wrecked or fallen off the world returns to its last gate. The race decides the match: the team in first place wins.

The same race, HUD and camera run on two kinds of maps: metre maps with colliders and grid maps with heroes. Controls, car physics and spline roads are shared. There are two sample games: the Oval Sprint oval and the Road Circuit along a spline road with trucks whose wheels roll and steer.
entries.verified: Bots complete three laps on both samples; a save in the middle of a race continues exactly as without it; other metre-map games play as before.
entries.limits: Getting in and the look of the cars still differ between the two map kinds: on metre maps cars are drawn as boxes.

entries.title: Client builds take only the engine modules they need
entries.summary: game.json can choose which optional engine parts go into the packaged game, or leave it to detection: "engineModules": ["auto"].
body: Every packaged game used to carry the whole engine: particles, Spine, gamepads, FBX and legacy model loaders, the city server client, traffic and map generation. Now a packaging.engineModules list, shared or per platform, can leave them out.

"auto" looks into the project: Spine and gamepad from game.json, particles from effect files, loaders from source models, simulations from rules and maps. If the game uses something excluded, the packager refuses with a clear error; without the field everything builds as before.

On a test macOS client build the executable shrank by about 7% just from linking only the code in use. Each disabled module removes from about a hundred kilobytes (gamepad) to a couple of megabytes (particles, legacy model loaders).
entries.verified: The packager checks the module choice for Web, Windows and macOS; sizes were measured on the macOS client.
entries.limits: HTML5 build size and startup are not measured yet: Emscripten was missing on the build machine. Android, iOS, Windows and Linux have not been built with modules off either.

entries.title: LENS: cameras as scene data, a Studio window and agent tools
entries.summary: A game's cameras are now described in one cameras.json file: several cameras, their draw order, their own render targets and frame capture. They can be created and edited in a Studio window or through the agent's MCP tools.
body: Each camera is a scene entity with its own components: transform, lens, follow rig, render target. The engine orders the cameras itself when one shows the image of another and warns about cycles.
Secondary cameras — monitors, picture-in-picture, portraits — get the same prepared frame as the main view: the game is not simulated again and animation does not step twice.

Studio has a cameras window: list, create, save and reload. Agents do the same through MCP: lens_scene_get, lens_camera_set and the related operations validate a change before writing and leave the working file intact on error. Any camera's frame can be saved to PNG.
entries.verified: The cameras window was opened in Studio on a Mac with a project and its camera loaded; the client with cameras enabled rendered the game scene on Metal. Replaying the frame into a secondary camera was compared pixel by pixel with the main frame on Metal.
entries.limits: The pixel comparison has only been run on Metal; Vulkan and mobile GPUs are not checked yet. Cost with many cameras has not been measured.

entries.title: GI probes: moment-based visibility instead of a plane
entries.summary: Probe visibility is stored as Chebyshev moments — the dark band on the Sponza arches is gone.

entries.title: Light baking: lightmaps and probes
entries.summary: The engine's own offline CPU path tracer writes lightmaps for static objects and terrain and a probe grid for everything that moves.
body: Map lights are marked mixed (stay realtime, their bounce is baked) or baked (lightmap and probes only). The runtime blends baked light with the realtime sun, like mixed lighting in Unity.

Rebakes are skipped when nothing changed: the bake stores a 64-bit hash of geometry, materials, textures, transforms, lights and settings. Available in the editor (Graphics → Light baking) and through MCP: lightbake_set, lightbake_bake, lightbake_status.
